strings: Deliver every packet. Keep every secret.
Tap a road for each numbered packet
Put the pieces back in number order
Follow the post office rules and keep secrets sealed
Have a class quest? Tap the four numbers from the board.
That is not a quest number. Check the board.
Tap the pieces in number order
Tap a packet or an empty slot
Packet {n} fell off the mail van!
Count the dots on each packet. Tap the damaged ones.
What goes wrong on this road
Start from where the packet is
Out of hops! Pick shorter ways.
The snoopy cat read packet {n}! Secrets go on sealed roads.
All packets are here. Tap the pieces in number order.
You already have packet {n}. That one is an extra copy.
Packet {n} is needed! Say got it instead.
Packet {n} does not match and was not sent again.
Not that one yet. What comes before it?
Too many rules! Keep only the ones the problems need.
{event} Nothing in your rules catches that.
Hint used: the third star is gone for this level
Skipped. You can come back to it later.
A picture is too big to send in one go. The network cuts it into small numbered packets. Each packet rides its own road, and the numbers put the picture back together at the other end.
Grandma wants a picture of an apple. Send each packet down the road, then rebuild the picture by number.
Where is the packet right now, and which road leaves from there?
The glowing road leads out of the office where the packet is waiting.
Tap the glowing road. When all the pieces have arrived, tap them in order: 1, then 2, then 3.
What does the network do with a big picture before sending it?
Sends it in one giant piece
Two roads lead to the school. Any open road is fine for a packet.
Does every packet have to take the same road?
Both glowing roads reach the school in two hops.
Tap either glowing road for each packet, then rebuild the picture by number.
Can two packets of one picture take different roads?
Four packets for the birthday house. One road is short and one is a long detour.
Which way reaches the house in the fewest hops?
The road over the hill is only two hops. The river way is three.
Tap the hill road, then the road into the house. Do that for every packet.
Which road is best for a packet?
The one with the most offices
Five packets for the zoo. Every road here meets at the center office.
Where do all the roads meet before the zoo?
Both first roads lead to the center office, and from there one road goes on.
Tap a glowing road, then the road to the center office, then the road to the zoo. Repeat for each packet.
How does the house know the order of the pieces?
By the number on each packet
By the color of the road
Six packets across the whole town. Three hops is the fewest for each one.
How many hops does the shortest way take?
The glowing roads are on a three hop way. Side roads between offices only add hops.
Tap the glowing road three times in a row for each packet, then place the six pieces by number.
A picture arrives as six packets. What happens at the house?
The pieces are put back in number order
Only the first piece is kept
Netville has many roads between its post offices. If one road is closed or busy, a packet simply takes another one. Packets can arrive in any order, so the numbers matter.
Cookies for the school! Watch the roads: one of them is about to close.
A road has closed. Is there another way to the school?
The river road is still open and it is just as short.
Tap the road to the river office, then the road into the school.
A road closes while you are sending. What do you do?
Send the next packets another way
One office is very busy today. Packets that pass it arrive late, so they may come in a mixed up order.
Why did a later packet arrive before an earlier one?
The busy office (with the clock) holds packets a while. The numbers still tell you the order.
Tap the pieces by number, not by the order they arrived: 1, 2, 3, 4.
Packet 3 arrives before packet 2. What now?
Wait, then place them in number order
Roadworks all over town. Two roads will close while you send. Keep finding a way.
When a road closes, which other roads still reach the zoo?
Follow the glowing roads: they always show an open way, even if it is one hop longer.
Tap the glowing road each time. The last packet needs four hops instead of three.
Why does Netville have more than one road between offices?
So packets still arrive when a road closes
A busy office and a road that closes. Six packets, three hops each, back in order at the end.
Which packets will arrive late, and does that change their numbers?
The busy office slows packets down. A closed road means another road. The numbers never change.
Take the glowing roads, then place the pieces 1 to 6 by their numbers.
What keeps a picture correct when its packets take different roads and arrive mixed up?
Hop budget! You may use thirteen hops in all. Four packets, three hops each, and a road that closes.
How many hops can each packet spend if the budget is thirteen for four packets?
Three hops each uses twelve. Only one spare hop. The glowing roads never waste one.
After the hill road closes, go by the river office and the mill office: still three hops.
Your hop budget is small. Which way do you pick?
The way with the fewest hops
The way with the most offices
This picture is a secret birthday plan. Open roads have a snoopy cat who reads every packet. Sealed roads cost two hops but nobody can peek.
Who can read a packet on an open road?
The roads with the lock are sealed. They cost more hops, but the snoopy cat sees nothing.
Tap the sealed road over the hill, then the sealed road into the house, for every packet.
Why send a secret on a sealed road even if it costs more?
Nobody on the way can read it
Post offices follow shared rules. When a packet arrives, the house says got it. When a packet is missing, the house asks for that number again. That way nothing stays lost.
Three packets were sent, but the mail van hit a bump. Say got it for each packet that arrived, and ask again for the one that did not.
Which packet number is missing from the board?
Slot 2 is empty. Packets 1 and 3 are waiting for a got it.
Tap packet 1, then Say got it. Tap slot 2, then Send again. Say got it for 2 and 3.
Packet 2 never arrives. What does the house send back?
Four packets this time. One got lost and one arrived twice! Extra copies go in the bin.
Can a picture use two copies of the same piece?
Packet 3 came twice. Say got it once, then throw the extra copy away. Slot 2 is empty.
Say got it for 1, 3 and 4. Throw away the second 3. Send again for 2, then say got it.
Packet 3 arrives twice. What do you do with the extra copy?

A protocol is a set of rules computers agree on before they talk: number every packet, say got it when one arrives, ask again for a missing one, throw away extra copies. Every post office in Netville follows them.
Five packets, two lost on the way. Acknowledge what arrived and ask again for the rest.
Which numbers never reached the house?
Slots 3 and 5 are empty. The sender will only resend what you ask for.
Say got it for 1, 2 and 4. Tap slot 3 and slot 5 and Send again, then say got it for both.
Shared rules computers follow to talk
A slow got it makes a sender resend too early. Now there are extra copies and one packet is still missing.
Why can the same packet arrive twice?
Packets 1 and 3 each came twice: one got it each, the copies go in the bin. Slot 4 is empty.
Say got it for 2, 1, 3 and 5. Throw away the extra 3 and the extra 1. Send again for 4, then say got it.
Why can a packet arrive twice?
The sender re-sent it when the got it was slow
Every packet carries a dot count. Count the dots on each one: if the count does not match, the packet was damaged and must be sent again.
Does the number of dots match what the label says on every packet?
Two packets have a label that does not match their dots.
Tap each packet whose dots do not match its label, then tap Check the mail.
What does counting the dots tell the house?
Whether a packet was damaged on the way
Before a big send, two computers shake hands in three steps. Put the steps in order.
What would you say first if you wanted to know someone is listening?
First ask if anyone is there. Then the answer. Then the sending starts.
Tap Hello, then Yes, then Great, sending now.
Why do two computers say hello before sending?
Yes! I am ready to receive.
Design the rule set. Three things go wrong on this road. Pick at most four rules that catch all of them.
Which rule tells the house that a packet is missing in the first place?
Numbers show the gap, got it tells the sender, ask again fills it, and copies need the bin.
Pick Number, Say got it, Ask again and Throw away copies. Then try the rules.
Just the rules the problems need
Say got it for each packet
Ask again for a missing packet
Send everything twice, just in case
Send the packets as loud as possible
The whole journey of a picture, in five rule cards. Put them in the order they happen.
What has to happen before a packet can pick a road?
Cutting comes first and rebuilding comes last. Roads before sending, got it after.
Tap Cut, Pick a road, Send, Say got it, Put back in order.
The packets go back in number order
Cut the picture into numbered packets
Pick a road for each packet
Send the packets on their way
Say got it, or ask again for a missing one
Put the packets back in number order
